questions.question: What is the naive probability formula for an event $A\subseteq S$?
When does naive probability apply?
options: When $S$ is infinite and uncountable
When outcomes have arbitrary unequal probabilities
When $S$ is finite and its outcomes are equally likely
When no sample space has been specified

questions.question: What does $|A|$ represent in the naive probability formula?
options: The probability of the whole sample space
The number of favorable outcomes in $A$
The number of outcomes outside $S$
The largest numerical outcome

questions.question: What does $|S|$ represent in the naive probability formula?
options: The number of favorable outcomes only, in every case without exception.
The probability assigned to $A$.
The complement of the event.
The total number of possible outcomes in the sample space

questions.question: When is the naive (equally likely) probability formula valid?
options: It works only when outcomes are equally likely
It works only for continuous random variables
It never uses counting
It always gives probability one

questions.question: What is the probability of rolling an even number on a fair die?
What is the probability of drawing an ace from a well-shuffled $52$-card deck?
If $S=\{1,2,3,4\}$ is equally likely and $A=\{1,4\}$, what is $P(A)$?
A fair coin is tossed twice. What is the naive probability of exactly one head?
Which example is appropriate for naive probability?
options: A uniformly chosen four-digit PIN from all four-digit PINs
A biased coin with unknown chance of heads
A waiting time with infinitely many possible values
A survey where different respondents have different sampling weights

questions.question: Why can counting errors cause probability errors in naive probability?
options: The numerator and denominator are counts used directly in the probability ratio
Counting errors are corrected automatically by equal likelihood
The denominator is never counted
The formula does not involve favorable outcomes

questions.question: Why is equal likelihood essential in naive probability?
options: Otherwise events cannot be subsets of $S$
Otherwise outcomes cannot simply be counted with equal weight
Otherwise the sample space cannot be finite, regardless of the specific input chosen.
Otherwise complements do not exist

questions.question: Which statement correctly separates sample space and event in naive probability?
options: $S$ supplies all possible outcomes; $A$ supplies the favorable outcomes
$A$ supplies all possible outcomes; $S$ supplies only failures
$S$ must have exactly one outcome
$A$ need not be a subset of $S$

questions.question: A fair six-sided die is rolled. What is the probability of rolling at least $5$?
A card is drawn uniformly from a $52$-card deck. What is the probability of drawing a heart?
A uniformly random digit from $\{0,\ldots,9\}$ is chosen. What is the probability it is odd?
Why is the formula $P(A)=|A|/|S|$ not valid for a biased coin modeled by $S=\{H,T\}$?
options: The sample space is not finite
The two outcomes are not equally likely
The event $A$ cannot be a subset of $S$
The formula requires exactly six outcomes

questions.question: If every outcome in a finite sample space is equally likely, what is the probability of a single outcome $\{\omega\}$?
A four-digit PIN is chosen uniformly from $0000$ to $9999$. What is the probability of choosing $0000$?
A fair die is rolled twice. What is the probability that the two rolls are equal?
